questions.prompt: Explain what an embedded system is, give examples, and contrast it with a general-purpose computer. [3]

questions.prompt: Explain why input devices are needed, give suitable choices for different data, and compare touch-screen methods. [3]

questions.prompt: Explain why output devices are needed, compare printer methods, and give suitable display or physical-output examples. [3]

questions.prompt: Explain primary storage, RAM and ROM, including their roles and whether contents remain without power. [3]

questions.prompt: Explain why secondary storage is needed and how saving and loading connect it to primary memory. [3]
questions.model: Secondary storage keeps saved programs and data more permanently. It retains data without power and is not directly accessed by the CPU. Load data into primary memory to process it; save a copy to keep it.

questions.prompt: Describe how magnetic, optical and solid-state storage work, giving an example of each. [3]

questions.prompt: Explain why virtual memory is used, how pages move, and why it can slow a computer. [3]
questions.model: Virtual memory uses secondary storage when available RAM is not enough. Pages are moved between RAM and virtual memory as they are needed. Page transfers take time; virtual memory does not increase physical RAM.

questions.prompt: Explain cloud storage, the physical equipment it uses, and the directions of uploading and downloading. [3]

questions.prompt: Compare local and cloud storage for a student who needs both offline access and shared files. [3]

questions.prompt: Explain what a NIC does, how it can be supplied, and when its manufacturer MAC address is assigned. [3]

questions.prompt: Explain a MAC address’s purpose, usual format and two parts. [3]

questions.prompt: Explain an IP address’s purpose, compare IPv4 with IPv6, and distinguish static from dynamic allocation. [3]

questions.prompt: Explain how a router forwards packets and how it can connect a local network and allocate addresses. [3]
